The energy-time uncertainty principle states that a finite lifetime \(\tau\) leads to an energy uncertainty (linewidth) \(\Delta E \approx \frac{\hbar}{\tau}\) (or \(\frac{h}{\tau}\) in some contexts). Using \(\hbar \approx 6.58 \times 10^{-16} \text{ eV·s}\):

- For \(\tau_1 = 10^{-9} \text{ s}\): \(\Delta E_1 \approx \frac{6.58 \times 10^{-16}}{10^{-9}} = 6.58 \times 10^{-7} \text{ eV}\).
- For \(\tau_2 = 10^{-8} \text{ s}\): \(\Delta E_2 \approx \frac{6.58 \times 10^{-16}}{10^{-8}} = 6.58 \times 10^{-8} \text{ eV}\).

To clearly distinguish the two energy levels, their energy difference must be larger than the combined or dominant linewidth. The broader level has an uncertainty of roughly \(6.6 \times 10^{-7} \text{ eV}\). Among the options:
(A) \(10^{-8} \text{ eV}\),
(B) \(10^{-4} \text{ eV}\),
(C) \(10^{-11} \text{ eV}\),
(D) \(10^{-9} \text{ eV}\),
only \(10^{-4} \text{ eV}\) is significantly larger than \(10^{-7} \text{ eV}\). Therefore, it is the only energy difference that allows clear resolution.

The proposed answer "10" is ambiguous, but the correct choice is (B) \(10^{-4} \text{ eV}\).

Answer: B
